questions.q: What is the peddler's central philosophical metaphor, and what specific life experience led him to formulate it?
questions.a: The peddler conceives the world as a giant rattrap that offers baits (riches, joys, shelter, food) to ensnare people, just as his rattraps offer cheese and pork to catch rats. He developed this idea during his "dreary ploddings" as a homeless vagabond who resorted to begging and petty thievery to "keep body and soul together." A wrong answer would treat the metaphor as a casual observation rather than a survival mechanism born of systemic rejection — revealing the student misses how the philosophy protects his dignity by reframing his victimhood as universal human condition.

questions.q: Explain why the peddler steals the crofter's thirty kronor despite receiving unprecedented hospitality. What does this reveal about his mindset at that point?
questions.a: The peddler steals because his rattrap philosophy has hardened into a self-fulfilling prophecy: he views kindness as merely another "bait" and cannot conceive of genuine altruism. The crofter's trust (showing the money pouch) becomes the ultimate bait — "the world had never been very kind to him, so it gave him unwonted joy to think ill of it." A wrong answer would cite mere poverty or greed, missing that the theft is an existential confirmation of his worldview: he steals to prove the world is a trap, not because he needs the money (he later discards it).

questions.q: Apply the concept of "dramatic irony" to the scene where the ironmaster mistakes the peddler for "Nils Olof." How does the peddler's internal monologue during this encounter differ from the ironmaster's perception?
questions.a: The ironmaster sees a long-lost regimental comrade fallen on hard times; the peddler sees an opportunity to exploit mistaken identity for "a couple of kronor." The irony deepens when the peddler thinks, "To go up to the manor house would be like throwing himself voluntarily into the lion's den" — he fears the trap (the law) while the ironmaster offers sanctuary. A student who only notes the mistaken identity misses the peddler's calculated performance: he adopts the "Captain von Stahle" persona strategically, revealing his agency even in degradation.

questions.q: Analyze the forest episode as an externalization of the peddler's internal state. How does the physical setting mirror his psychological condition after the theft?
questions.a: The forest becomes an "impenetrable prison" with paths that "twisted back and forth" — a literal maze mirroring his mental entrapment in his own philosophy. Having stolen the bait (money), he now experiences the trap's closure: "He had let himself be fooled by a bait and had been caught." The December darkness, cold, and exhaustion parallel his moral desolation. A superficial answer would describe the forest as just a setting; the analytical answer shows how Lagerlöf uses pathetic fallacy to make the peddler's abstract metaphor physically manifest.

questions.q: Evaluate Edla Willmansson's intervention as the catalyst for the peddler's redemption. Is her compassion naive or strategically transformative? Defend with textual evidence.
questions.a: Edla's compassion is strategically transformative, not naive. She perceives his fear ("Either he has stolen something or else he has escaped from jail") yet insists, "You may be sure, Captain, that you will be allowed to leave us just as freely as you came." This unconditional offer — dignity without demand — shatters his rattrap worldview. The proof: he returns the money, leaves a rattrap as gift, and signs as "Captain von Stahle," claiming the identity the ironmaster falsely assigned him. A weak evaluation calls her "kind"; a strong one shows she weaponizes kindness as the only force that can break a self-fulfilling prophecy of entrapment.

questions.q: Create a 60-word diary entry from the peddler's perspective on Christmas night at Ramsjö, capturing his internal shift using the rattrap metaphor. Use first-person voice and include one direct textual echo.
questions.a: A strong entry: "The trap snapped shut — but not on me. Edla's kindness was no cheese-rind; it was a key. I lay on the sofa, sleeping 'as quietly and safely' as never before. The thirty kronor burn in my pocket like coals. Tomorrow I return them. I am no rat. I am Captain von Stahle." A weak entry summarizes plot without metaphorical internalization or textual echo ("quietly and safely" from the text).
